content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes dealing with grasping motion generation for a dexterous hand from human demonstrations. The authors leverage a generative model architecture composed of conditional variational autoencoder, where they are able to generate different and continuous grasping motion plans. The key idea is to compute the latent distributions from targeted input (robot hand demonstrations, object point cloud and time sequence) based on which different grapsable motion trajectory can be sampled in inference stage. The experimental results suggest that the proposed model allows generalization to grasp multiple and unseen objects in sim2real scenario.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. As far as I aware, this is a novel and interesting idea overall. The paper techniques aim to learn a continuous grasping process for dexterous robots hands.
2. Detailed experiments to verify the feasibility of this approach.
2. The paper is clearly written and is easy to follow. A robotic researcher with some knowledge of generative model(VAE, GAN) should be able to reimplement the methods in this work.

Weakness:
1. The video and figures show the experimental setting is about 'solo-object' grasping. I am not sure if the approach can be scaled to multi-object or complex scenes with obstacles, as it does not consider collision or unintended contact either.
2. As paper proposes, this approach needs to sample lots of grasps from the latent distribution and then select the successful trajectories in the simulator to test in real world. The parameter of sampled quantity is 10000 as mentioned in 'Implementation Details' section. How long will it take to filter out all successful trajectories in simulation? What's the effectiveness of this parameter setting to final evaluations?
3. I am concerned about the appropriateness of the conference for this paper. The paper does not propose a new robotic learning method but rather integrates a marginally novel network structure(CVAE) for learning to grasp. There are some other additional works[1] also follow the idea of learning embedding space to encode the demontrations plans by conditioned generative model. So it may be a better choice to submit a revised version to robotics conference or journal, e.g. IROS, RAL.  
4. Comparing to traditional RL approaches would make it a more fair empirical study.
5. I believe that a comparison of CGF's and baselines' model inference speed could improve the quality of this paper.
6. I believe that t-sne visualization of the CVAE embedded space could help readers understand the motion states better.

[1] 'Hierarchical Policies for Cluttered-Scene Grasping With Latent Plans'
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The author has provided implementation details, simulation environment, and real robot setup, and has committed to release their code and environment.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper presents an interesting idea for the robot hand imitation learning with some novelties, but the scope may not align well with this conference as there is no fundamental novelty on the learning method.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors leverage human demonstrations to learn smooth, continuous grasping behavior. Instead of learning a motion imitation policy, the authors propose the continuous grasping function, which is a motion planning network which can be used to sample various plausible grasping trajectories given a target object point cloud. The authors evaluate their proposed method in simulation and demonstrate better smoothness and success rate than many baselines, and deploy the learned trajectories to a real robot.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strengths of the paper:
1) A novel idea for imitation based motion generation in high dimensional tasks such as grasping. 
2) Good performance and smoothness of motions compared with many baselines. 
3) Able to zero-shot sim-real transfer on hardware.
4) Generalize to novel objects.

The weaknesses of the paper:
1) If I understand it correctly, the main module is an offline motion planner: the authors have to sample many trajectories and pick the best one for the current hand pose and object type. Then a closed-loop tracking is performed on the fixed trajectory. Some baselines actually have an advantage of generating new grasping trajectories on the fly, even for the real robot.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is novel and clearly written. The results are well supported through comparison with different baselines and ablation studies.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper provides a novel idea to solve motion planning for high dimensional manipulation tasks and demonstrates great potential for human-like grasping. It is mostly clearly written and well evaluated in both sim and real.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors present an approach to transfer human multi-finger grasping demonstrations to real-robots. The proposed approach consists in retargeting human demonstrations into robot demonstrations. This is possible assuming that the demonstrations contain information about hand-joint positions which are mapped into the corresponding robot hand joints. The mapped motions are then encoded into a Continuous Grasping Function (CGF), which is a VAE for joint positions conditioned on time and object point-cloud. At inference time, the measured object point-cloud is fed to the CFG and time values are used to unroll joint positions trajectories. The resulting trajectories are differentiated twice to obtain their first and second derivatives, useful as references for an inverse dynamics (ID) tracking controller. Experiments in sim and on a real robot show that the proposed approach performs better than GraspTTA/GraspIT+RRT/CEM-MPC in terms of: smoothness of trajectories (sim), cost per success (sim) and grasp success (real robot). Authors perform an ablation study to compare the proposed ID approach with the default PD control in simulation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: The paper considers a very important problem, i.e. how to use human demonstrations in multi-finger manipulation tasks. The proposed approach is relatively straightforward and relies on pre-existing datasets. One of the strengths of the paper is to benchmark the proposed approach on real robot experiments (task: 20 attempts to grasp and lift 6 standard objects).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is relatively clear but some parts could benefit a thorough review. The quality of the paper is acceptable but the scientific novelty relatively minor. Reproducibility is always a concern in real robot experiments and it is poorly addressed in this paper (e.g. no details on the used sensors, their mounting position, etc.).
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper gives a relatively minor contribution w.r.t. the current state of the art. My assessment is "marginally below the acceptance threshold" but not too far from "reject, not good enough". Additionally, there are some minor comments hereafter.

- Section 3.2. From what described in the paper, the used hand has 3 fingers while human demonstrators have 5 fingers. Authors do not seem to describe in detail the mapping and the limitation in mapping from 5 fingers to 3 fingers.

- Figure 3. The picture quality is low and authors should invest some time in improving it. It's unclear what is represented in the staked-pictures on the left-most and right-most part of the figure (my guess: left-most is the DexYCB dataset, right-most cartesian coordinates of the joints). Time $tis displayed as vertical bar divided in three subparts and it's unclear what these three parts represent. 

- Page 4. "inputs; During" -> fix typo

- Table 1. Numbers on the table don't have a unit of measure and authors don't give details on how they have been computed. 

- Table 2 and Section 4.3. Authors never say what "cost" means (e.g. FLOPS, computation time).

- Section 4.5. It's unclear what this ablation study is useful for. The proposed inverse dynamics (also know as computed torque) has well-known robustness properties with respect to variation of the dynamics. PD controller are well-know to be less robust to similar variations. So this whole sections doesn't seem to be an interesting ablation study.

The authors samples the grasping plans in simulator and then transfer to a real-robotic arm.

- The application demo helps to understand effectiveness of the method.
- Real-world demo of the method is a big plus.

- The paper is not well-written and has lots of ambiguous statements.
